newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl ally calls for tax hike to finance budget gap. [CORRECTED 22:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Kohl ally calls for tax hike to finance budget gap. [CORRECTED 22:30 GMT]

text.p: German taxes must be raised to help plug a gap in next year's budget, a political ally of Chancellor Helmut Kohl said in remarks published on Sunday.

Heiner Geissler, deputy parliamentary leader (corrects title) of Kohl's Christian Democrats, told Bild am Sonntag: "We need fiscal clearance which will create more jobs. The value added tax should be raised by at least one percentage point."
In August Kohl promised the value-added tax would not be raised before the next parliamentary session begins late 1998.
On Friday, the government agreed to defer a one percentage cut in the 7.5 percent solidarity tax to finance German unification and planned for 1997.
The deal is expected to generate 3.7 billion marks in savings but finance minister Theo Waigel said another three billion marks needs to be saved through spending cuts.
Meanwhile the three coalition partners continued to bicker about the size of the solidarity surchage cut.
Hermann Otto Solms, parliamentary leader of Kohl's junior coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP), told Bild am Sonntag "the surcharge will be reduced by two percentage points to 5.5 percent in 1998."

But Erwin Huber, Christian socialist (CSU) party member and finance minister in Bavaria, told the same newspaper "in light of the difficult tax situation it will be possible to cut the solidarity tax by only one percentage point in 1998."
After surviving a round of regional elections largely on promises to cut taxes earlier this year, the Free Democrats have incurred public wrath for breaking their word this week.

"The Betrayers from Bonn," screamed Bild Zeitung am Sonntag's front page headline, reminding readers the Free Democrats had scored a major coup earlier this year by persuading the coalition partners to lower the tax next year.
FDP members justified their decision by saying they chose the lesser of several evils including a tax hike or a possible collapse of the coalition.
"We did not want such an unprepared break in the coalition, and that is why I agreed to the plan," Juergen Moellemann, a regional FDP party head told Bild am Sonntag.
Wolfgang Gerhard, head of the FDP, told an audience in Stuttgart on Saturday: "This was the only chance. Otherwise I would have had to justify a increase in taxes."

Finance Minister Theo Waigel too was criticised for his part in the deal with Welt am Sonntag worrying that Waigel's habit of patching up holes with solutions thrown together quickly "was becoming ever less serious."

"If the coalition reneged on plans to cut the solidarity tax, what will happen Chancellor Kohl's promise to not raise the valued added-tax before the next election?" the newspaper wrote in an editorial.
